summary: Evidence is adjacent but substantive: controlled studies show that trace and hierarchical visualizations can improve particular comprehension tasks, while architecture-documentation research warns that format alone may not improve understanding. No direct controlled study located evaluates the full generated companion-app bundle.

items.text: A Controlled Experiment for Program Comprehension through Trace Visualization — Bas Cornelissen, Andy Zaidman, and Arie van Deursen (2011). Participants using a trace visualization completed tasks 22% faster and answered 43% more correctly in the reported experiment. This supports runtime-linked views, but the treatment was one visualization rather than an integrated companion product.

Software Landscape and Application Visualization for System Comprehension with ExplorViz — Florian Fittkau, Alexander Krause, and Wilhelm Hasselbring (2017). Four controlled experiments found hierarchical and multi-level visualizations improved correctness for several comprehension comparisons, with task- and representation-specific effects. This directly supports layered landscape views but not automatically generated prose or decision links.

A Study of Documentation for Software Architecture — Neil A. Ernst and Martin P. Robillard (2023). In a randomized questionnaire study with 65 participants, structured versus narrative documentation had no significant association with answer quality; prior source familiarity dominated. This is important counter-evidence: navigability and structure do not substitute for links to code and task-relevant evidence.
